name: Barban
lead: Two Defranceschi families in 1945, and the parish where the surname still appears in Croatian records today.
body: Acta Croatica records surviving Defranceschi households in the Labin area at Barban into the present century — one of only four Croatian places where the name is still found.

name: Cerovlje
lead: The municipality Gologorica sits in today.
body: Included here because modern Croatian administration files Gologorica under Cerovlje, so civil records after 1945 are found under this name rather than the village's own.

name: Gologorica
lead: The family's documented seat. A De Franceschi house of 1711 still stands on the main square.
body: Municipality of Cerovlje, central Istria. Roman material has been found here, including a gravestone now in the Pazin museum. The parish church of Saints Peter and Paul carries Renaissance altars and a seventeenth-century baptismal font, and a small Romanesque chapel of the Blessed Virgin keeps fifteenth-century frescoes.
Carlo De Franceschi, the historian, was born here in 1809 — of modest landowners, in his own biographer's phrase, not of gentry. In October 1945 the village still held two Defranceschi families.

registers.note: The six undigitised books are the oldest — baptisms 1644–1763, marriages 1656–1781, burials 1646–1777.

name: Gračišće
lead: Eight household censuses across 150 years — the richest register series found anywhere in this project.
body: First recorded in 1199. Held by the Patriarch of Aquileia, then the counts of Gorizia, and from 1374 part of the Duchy of Pazin. Bishop Paskazije of Pićan consecrated the Gothic chapel here in 1486, in his own birthplace.
Glagolitic and Latin graffiti survive scratched into the chapel interior — Croatian, written in Croatian letters, inside a town the maps called Gallignana.

registers.note: Thirty-one of thirty-two books digitised. The status animarum give house-by-house listings roughly every twenty years.

name: Ližnjan
lead: Named by the existing family research as the origin of a line that went to the United States and Germany — and never worked in an archive.
body: The received account gives Ližnjan as one of four directions the family dispersed in, onward to the United States and Germany. No register work has been done on it, and the 1945 census records no Defranceschi household here — which does not disprove the line, but does mean it had already gone by then.
Twenty-four registers survive, baptisms from 1683. Only fourteen are digitised, the lowest proportion of any parish in this study.

name: Motovun
lead: One family in 1945 — and 121 of 122 registers digitised, the most complete series in the study.
body: A Venetian hill town whose registers open in 1586. If a link has to be traced through the western, Venetian half of Istria, this is the easiest parish in which to do it.

name: Pazin
lead: A De Franceschi household in the county town in 1684 — a hundred and seven years earlier than this archive had it, and fifty-six years before Kobler's man leaves for Fiume.
body: **«Die 24 huius — Ego qui supra baptizavi Mariam filiam legitimam Francisci de Franceschi et uxoris eius Marinę. Patrini fuerunt Hilarius Celin[?] et Jacoba eiusdem…»** Pazin, *Births 1582, 1614–1624, 1645, 1643–1685*, baptism of **24 March 1684**, read off the film at full magnification on 13 September 2026.

Until then the earliest record of the name at Pazin here was **1791** — two elaborate Latin names, Conraddus Vincentius and Liberatus Francus Xaverius, in a single household. This is a century earlier and it is a family: a father, a wife, a legitimate daughter, two godparents standing.

Its weight is not its age. **Kobler has a Giovanni Battista reaching Fiume from the County of Pazin «intorno al 1740»** — the sentence the whole Fiume argument hangs on — and nobody has ever looked for that man at the end he left from. There is now a documented De Franceschi household in the county town fifty-six years before the date Kobler gives. That is not a connection and is not claimed as one; it is the first time the question can be put to a real household rather than to an assumption.

The index gets this entry wrong twice. It transcribes the surname as «De Francesch», dropping the *-i* the page plainly writes, and it puts **Jacoba — a godparent — into the mother's field**. The mother is **Marina**.
Seven indexed records in all, six of them ours, 1684 to 1859. Six volumes of parish book, the oldest opening in **1582**, and only one page of them has been read here.

name: Pićan
lead: The diocese Gologorica and Gračišće belonged to — but not the custodian of their registers.
body: A tiny bishopric with an outsized place in Istrian church history; in the Middle Ages both ecclesiastical and secular power at Pićan lay with the Patriarchs of Aquileia. Its own registers run from 1664 and are almost entirely digitised. One Defranceschi family was counted here in 1945.

name: Poreč
lead: Where Camillo De Franceschi was born in 1868, and where his father published L'Istria in 1879.
body: The Gologorica branch reached Poreč before it reached Crikvenica. It is also the seat of the diocesan archive that holds the later registers for half the parishes in this study.

name: Seget
lead: An estate south of Umag, bought in 1720 by a de Franceschi family two generations out of Crete.
body: Venice granted the land in 1604 to families fleeing Greece and Montenegro. Captain Vincenzo Cuchich of Šibenik sold it in 1623 to the Venier of Venice, who held it a century and made it a working estate. In 1720 Nicolò and Marc'Antonio de Franceschi, sons of Giorgio, bought all of Catarina Bernardo Venier's Istrian property; in 1730 Umag made them citizens, them and their heirs.

They had reached Istria fleeing Crete after the Candian War of 1669. A monograph on the estate records that the family had two branches in Istria — one at Gologorica, one at Umag and Seget — and that family archives survive from both. One De Franceschi household was still counted at Seghetto in the 1945 census.

name: Svetvinčenat
lead: The oldest De Franceschi household in Istria this archive can date: a baptism of 21 December 1628, thirty-eight years before the cluster everyone knew about.
body: **«Alì 21 Decembre — Elena fiola di Francescho di Franceschi et di Eufemia sua consorte fu batezata da me piovano sopra deto. Fu compare s.r Zan Piero Quelo. Comare Chiara consorte di Tomaso Ostricich.»** Svetvinčenat, Births 1589–1646, image 58, read off the film on 13 September 2026.

Until that morning this archive dated the family here from **1666** — Colotta in October, Fioretta in November, two children to the font in one autumn. The 1628 entry puts a whole household here a generation and a half earlier, with a wife, a daughter and two godparents out of the parish's own gentry. It is a settled family, not an arrival.

It also reorders Istria. The earliest dated occurrences ran Labin 1615, Moncalvo di Pisino 1661, Svetvinčenat 1666. They now run **Labin 1615, Svetvinčenat 1628, Moncalvo 1661** — and the sentence this archive wrote about the family reaching Svetvinčenat five years after Moncalvo has it backwards by thirty-three.

It is one entry, though. The 1589–1646 book holds **one** De Franceschi record in fifty-seven years; the 1568–1588 book and the 1581–1623 marriage book hold none. And nothing joins Francescho to the Nadal, Batta, Anto, Andrea and Gaspo of the 1660s and 70s — thirty-eight years is one long generation or two short ones, and no entry says which.

Across six of its nine parish books the parish yields **118 indexed records** of the name, from 1628 to 1887. Nineteen are marriages, eight of them daughters marrying out. One name recurs at both ends: a **Quelo** stands godfather in 1628, and a **Quelis** — Andriana, wife of the canon Ottavio — stands godmother to Nardo's son in 1707.

name: Umag
lead: The hamlet of Seghetto held one De Franceschi family in 1945. Every one of Umag's 128 registers is digitised.
body: The only parish in this study with a complete digitisation — 128 of 128 books, marriages from 1602. Whatever is here can be read from anywhere.

name: Vižinada
lead: Twenty-three records from 1750, and the parish where the Kaštelir family's children were born.
body: Vižinada holds the name from **1750**, when a Mathæus De Franceschi «of Anton» is buried, and carries it to 1877 — twenty-three records of ours out of twenty-four indexed, across nine volumes opening in 1663.

It is one parish of three. **Francesco Napoleone De Franceschi was baptised here on 7 September 1818**, son of **Giulio and Maria Ceselin**; both father and son then appear in the Kaštelir register, and the next generation again at Tar. See Kaštelir for the household as a whole.

Vižinada also carries the parish of **Kaštelir** in its own books, which is why the death of Mathaeus De Franceschi in 1819 — the one entry this archive found on film 005497893 — is catalogued under Vižinada and took place at Castellier. That confusion cost a day in September and is worth keeping in view.
**And Vižinada is why Draguč looked real.** FamilySearch's place parameter returns the two parishes' record sets identically; Draguč's twenty-five entries were these.

name: Vodnjan
lead: Twelve Defranceschi families in 1945, and — since 9 September 2026 — five documented generations behind them. The best-attested cluster in southern Istria, read out of a register nobody has indexed.
body: The 1945 cadastre counts twelve Defranceschi families at Vodnjan, against two at Gologorica and one at Gračišće. For most of this archive's life that was all it knew, and the twelve households were listed as its second open question.

They are not open any more. The parish books of Dignano — FamilySearch catalogue item koha:963267 — hold baptisms from 1815, marriages 1815–1884 and deaths to 1893. The baptism register gives eight households between 1816 and 1865. **The marriage register has never been indexed by anybody**, and was read here opening by opening.

What came out of it: a line five generations deep, from a **Pietro** standing behind a marriage of the 1770s, through **Gio. Maria De Franceschi and Michiela Zambaletta**, to their children **Pietro, Cristoforo and Veniera** and the grandchildren married off in the 1820s. A **second, separate line** descending from a Domenico. **Four women of the name married out before the books open** — Domenica, Antonia Maria, Lucia and Veniera — recoverable only because their daughters' weddings named their mothers. And one household of three brothers, all «di Giuseppe»: **Don Stefano the priest**, who witnessed sixteen weddings under the parroco Giovanni Tromba, and **Pietro the ploughman and Cristoforo the weaver**, who signed the same book with a cross.

The town's church paperwork ran to the **Ordinariate of Pola**; the banns could be waived by the **Imperial-Royal Circle Captaincy**. Weddings involving Vodnjan people were also held at **Šišan** and **Svetvinčenat**, and a «Matt.o de Franceschi da Dignano» was buried at **Rovinj** in 1728 — the same formula, ninety-six years apart, naming the town only from outside it.

name: Čepić
lead: One family in 1945. The youngest register series in the study — nothing before 1782.
body: Recorded in the 1945 cadastre as Ceppici di Pòrtole, in the Motovun judicial district.

name: Crikvenica
lead: Named for a church: the Pauline monastery of 1412, in the deed that first records the name.
body: Nikola IV Frankopan gave the monastery to the Pauline fathers on 14 August 1412. The order stayed four hundred years, until Joseph II dissolved it in 1786, and for that whole time it was Vinodol's school, pharmacy and library.

A harbour came in 1877, a bathing beach in 1888, the first hotel in 1891 — a Vinodol village that became an Austrian seaside resort inside one lifetime. The Gologorica branch reached here by way of Poreč.

registers.note: Župa Crikvenica, 1798–1908, filmed from the Croatian State Archives. The register begins twelve years after Joseph II dissolved the Pauline monastery that gave the town its name.

name: Rijeka
lead: The largest documented concentration of the surname anywhere in Croatia — 447 records, once Vitipolis is recognised for what it is.
body: The indexed church books give 225 records under Fiume, 178 under Vitipolis and 44 under Rijeka. They are the same city. Vitipolis is the Latin for the city of Saint Vitus — Rijeka's patron, and the saint its cathedral is named for — which is also what the German Sankt Veit am Flaum means. Read together they make Rijeka the single biggest cluster of this family in the country, larger than Pola, Poreč and Omiš combined.

This is where the received account puts three separate arrivals: Domenico from 1614, Valentino out of Carnia made a citizen in 1739, and Giovanni Battista from the County of Pazin around 1740. The registers show de Franceschi children being baptised here from 1626.

registers.note: 447 indexed records under three names for one city.

name: Senj
lead: An Uskok garrison on the Habsburg Military Frontier — never Italian, unlike Istria.
body: Taken over by the Habsburgs in 1522 as a state-controlled Militärgrenze, and from the 1530s the base of the Uskoks, the refugee raiders who fought the Ottomans and Venice until an agreement between Habsburg and Venice expelled them in 1617. The Nehaj fortress was built by the Uskok captain Ivan Lenković in 1558.
Records for Senj fall to the State Archives in Rijeka, whose remit covers Primorje-Gorski Kotar plus the city of Senj. That inventory is not yet mapped.

registers.note: The Kvarner gap is now partly closed. FamilySearch holds microfilm of the Senj parish registers 1734–1920 and of Sv. Juraj near Senj 1695–1868, filmed from the Croatian State Archives in Zagreb — plus an Austrian army field-hospital register for 1805–06. The DARI collection itself still has no published parish-level inventory.

name: Mione
lead: A hundred and thirty people at 710 metres — and the Italian end of a documented migration into Istria.
body: First written on 15 June 1185, when Odolrico called Gusetto, Strabo, and Vecellone, son-in-law of Giovanni da Mione, received concessions from Domenico, abbot of Moggio. An independent comune until 1871, now a frazione of Ovaro in the Canale di Gorto.

A stone above the village, at some 1,600 metres, carries Venetic inscriptions — this valley was a route long before it was a parish. From the parishes of Ovaro and Luincis a long series of weavers took the road into Istria; the documents become numerous in the seventeenth century and frequent in the eighteenth.

registers.note: Confirmed dead end: FamilySearch holds only the Napoleonic civil registration for Ovaro's frazioni — Mione, Luincis, Luìnt, Muina, Ovasta, Liariis, Entrampo, Lenzone, Agrons e Cella, Cludinico, Muscletto, Chialina — filmed from the Archivio di Stato di Udine. There are no Ovaro parish books on film anywhere online. The pre-1806 church registers must be asked for at the parish.

name: Imotski
lead: Taken from the Ottomans in July 1717 with a De Franceschi first over the wall. The family has been here three hundred years.
body: Of the seventy Venetians living at Imotski after 1717, only the de Franceschi settled permanently in the Imotska krajina. They held the Perinuša estate — the former begluk of arci-beg Čaušević, with land, houses, a mill and a tower on the Vrljika — and they are still present, physically and in the town's memory, though most of the arable land and the mills are gone and many members have scattered.

There is a long local antagonism to go with it: a persistent belief that the liberation was owed solely to the Imotski Franciscans and the people, which casts the acquisition of Perinuša as a seizure. The estate had in fact been Ottoman crown land, held by begs; who owned it before that is lost in medieval darkness.
Fewer than five people named Franceschi live at Imotski today.

held: FamilySearch film, from HDA Zagreb and Zadar
registers.note: The Podjezerja book runs 1693–1733 and so spans the siege of 1717 itself; Imotski-Glavina picks up in 1731. Both were filmed from the Croatian State Archives.

name: Omiš
lead: A former pirate town at the Cetina mouth, and the Dalmatian family's first seat — a De Franceschi owned a warship here by 1590.
body: The de Franceschi are said to have reached Dalmatia in the fourteenth century as an influential Italian noble house, and to have established themselves at Omiš, where Gaspar de Franceschi is recorded in 1590 as owner of the warship Vascello and later admiral of the fleet.

Zuane Ivan Franceschi sat on the town council here, and it was as an Omiš councillor that he pressed the Imotski refugees' case with the Venetian Provveditore Generale. His estate at Dobrč — today Pisak, along the coast — is where he sheltered them from January 1715.

registers.note: Župa Omiš, 1588–1894. The series opens two years before Gaspar de Franceschi is recorded here as owner of the warship Vascello, which makes this the one place where the Dalmatian family's earliest claim can actually be tested.

name: Split
lead: Twenty-five Franceschi — the largest single concentration of any spelling of this name anywhere in Croatia.
body: Acta Croatica records about sixty people named Franceschi in Croatia today, in thirty households, against fifty in the middle of the last century — an increase of twenty per cent. They are Croats, from Split, and most were born at Split or Imotski.

This is the mirror image of the Istrian story. The Defranceschi of the Pazin area have fallen from about fifty mid-century to about ten; the Franceski of Rijeka from thirty to a single household. Only the Dalmatian branch is growing.

name: Rovinj
lead: The name from 1619 — and the man «da Dignano» buried at Christmas 1728, three weeks after his wife.
body: Rovinj carries the name from **1619**, when a **Pietro De Franceschi** is buried — the entry this archive holds from another direction as «morì ser Piero di Franceschi da Pola», 27 May 1619, and its earliest dated Istrian record until the Svetvinčenat baptism of 1628 was found.

It does **not** carry it from 1569. The 1569, 1583 and 1592 entries that a surname search returns are **Fracischetto**, **Francoscheto** and **Franceschero** — three other families, and a caution against reading a fuzzy match as a date.

The household that can be followed is **Mattio De Franceschi and Elisabetta**, who baptise **Martino in 1722** and **Benedetto on 23 October 1726**. **Isabetta is buried on 4 December 1728 and Matto on the 27th of the same month** — three weeks apart. And the archive already held that second entry from outside: «**Ob.to di Matt.o de Franceschi da Dignano**». A man described by the Rovinj priest as *from Dignano* had been in the town long enough to baptise two sons there, and buried his wife three weeks before he was buried himself. That the Isabetta of 4 December is the wife rather than a daughter is an inference from the 1722 and 1726 entries, not a statement of the register.
Twenty-one records of ours out of twenty-five indexed, 1619 to 1864, across **twenty-nine volumes opening in 1553** — the largest unread register in Istria that carries the name.

name: Pula
lead: The see and the port at the foot of Istria — and the town a De Franceschi is called «da Pola» from, in 1619.
body: Carlo's own *L'Istria* lists Franceschi among the noble families of Pola «venuti da Capodistria» before the plague of 1631 — which makes Pula one of the two candidate parents for the southern Istrian clusters, the other being Koper itself.
The earliest dated record this archive holds in Istria names a man of this town rather than of the one he was buried in: **«ser Piero di Franceschi da Pola»**, buried at Rovinj on 27 May 1619.

Pula is also where the church paperwork of the whole south ran. The marriage dispensations entered in the Vodnjan register are issued by the **Ordinariate of Pola** — «dell'Ordinariato di Pola» — and that is the office to write to for what those registers only allude to.

name: Kaštelir
lead: Seventeen records, and — read together with Vižinada and Tar — one family across three parishes.
body: Kaštelir was for a year the densest thing in Istria this archive could document and could not explain: seventeen records of the name, four of them accepted, a hilltop village kept under Vižinada, and no lane on the branch chart running through it.

Read by image rather than by place text, the three parishes of the Poreč hinterland turn out to hold **the same people**. **Giulio (Julius) De Franceschi × Maria Ceselin** — the name is written Ceselin, Sesalin and Cedelini in three different hands — has a son **Francesco Napoleone baptised at Vižinada on 7 September 1818**, a daughter **Catharina baptised at Kaštelir in 1829**, and is himself buried at **Kaštelir on 19 September 1854**, entered as «Giulio Defranceschi, of Mattio». **Francesco Napoleone** then raises his own family at Kaštelir with **Maria Radojković** — Aloisia 1859, Josephus 1862, Margarita 1869.

A second household runs alongside it: **Angelus Defranceschi × Lucia-Antonia Rodella**, whose son **Julius is baptised at Kaštelir on 29 January 1866** and **buried at Tar on 9 March 1870**, aged four. Angelus dies at Tar in 1895.

The join is by name, date and parish adjacency — no single document names two of these places at once — so it is an inference, and is marked as one. But it is the first time the hinterland has read as a family rather than as a scatter.

And it corrects this page's neighbour: **Draguč, long counted at twenty-five records, holds none.** Its three volumes were fetched and every image tested. The twenty-five were Vižinada's, returned twice by a search parameter that does not filter.

name: Bakar
lead: The deep-water bay east of Rijeka, and one of the Kvarner parishes where the surname sits in the registers with no line yet attached to it.
body: Bakar belongs with Rijeka and Ledenice in the group of Kvarner parishes this archive can name people in but cannot yet join to any line. The households here are treated as **unplaced** — documented, and honestly unattached — rather than folded into the Carnia or Pazin-county descent on the strength of a shared surname.

name: Draguč
lead: Twenty-five records that were never here.
body: This archive's parish table has carried **Draguč, 25 records, 1784–1851** since September. On 13 September 2026 the parish's three volumes were fetched from FamilySearch and every image in them tested against a pool of 1,768 indexed records of the name. **None matched.**

The twenty-five were **Vižinada's**. FamilySearch's place parameter is a relevance boost and not a filter, and the two parishes return the same records in the same order — a thing this archive tested and published on 9 September, then went on using the number anyway for four more days.

Draguč is left on the map because the correction is worth more than the deletion. Its books exist and open in 1784; nothing says the name cannot be in an unindexed page of them. What is settled is that **nothing in the index puts it here**.

name: Premantura
lead: The last village before the cape at the bottom of Istria, and one of the southern parishes the surname holds in.
body: Premantura sits with Ližnjan, Fažana, Šišan and Vodnjan in the southern Istrian group. The households here are documented in the sweeps but not yet worked through a register page by page, which is the only method that has produced generations in this part of Istria.

name: Fažana
lead: Forty-two records, every one of them ours — and most of what this archive has been calling the Pula cluster.
body: Fažana has been a single dot on the branch chart reading «baptisms and deaths at Fasana through the 1810s, 1840s and after». Read by image it holds **forty-two records of the name between 1770 and 1855, and not one of them belongs to another family** — a cleaner return than any Istrian parish except Ližnjan.

Two households. **Vittorio De Franceschi × Stella Tamborin** — written Etella, Steffa and Samburin by four different hands — baptise Perina on 23 April 1810, Vittorio in 1813, and **Natale Mattio on 21 April 1816**. **Giuseppe De Franceschi × Giovanna Beluzzi** baptise Elisabetta in 1810 and **Irene on 13 October 1816**; a Giovanna «of Giuseppe Defranceschi» is buried as early as 1770.

Those names matter. This archive's sweep table names the **Pula** cluster's people as «Natale Mattio, Angelo, Vitorio, Elisabetta, Irene De Franceschi». **Natale Mattio, Vittorio, Elisabetta and Irene are Fažana's**, four miles up the coast — another town-name supplied by a search that could not see a town.
One entry keeps two surnames at once: **«Petrina Tamburin or Defranceschi», 1807.**

name: Telve
lead: In the Valsugana, east of Trento — the largest single concentration of the name outside Istria and Dalmatia in this archive's roster.
body: Twenty-two people of the surname in this archive sit at Telve, more than at any Istrian village except Vodnjan. They come out of David's family tree rather than out of a register this archive has read, and **no descent connects them to the Istrian or Carnian families**. Defranceschi is a common Trentino surname formed independently from the same patronymic; that is the working assumption here and it is an assumption, not a finding.
Telve is listed so the twenty-two are visible and counted, not folded into a line they may have nothing to do with.

name: Laives
lead: South of Bolzano in the Adige valley — a second Tyrolean cluster, and like Telve unattached to any Istrian line.
body: Eleven people of the name, from the family tree rather than from a register read here. Laives belongs with Telve, Strigno and Fiera di Primiero in the Trentino–South Tyrol group: same surname, different formation, **no documented connection to Istria**.

name: Strigno
lead: A Valsugana village a few kilometres from Telve, with the same surname and the same open question.
body: Grouped with Telve and Fiera di Primiero. Counted here rather than absorbed into an Istrian line.

name: Torrington
lead: A brass town in the Naugatuck valley of Connecticut, and the largest American landing-place in this archive.
body: Twelve people of the name in Torrington. The New England brass and clock towns took Istrian and Trentino labour in the same decades that Brooklyn took the Gallignana families, and this is where a cluster of them settled.
Nothing here has yet been checked against a federal census or a naturalisation file. **That is the next step for this place**, and it is the method that worked for the Eleven in Brooklyn.

name: Pfullingen
lead: Below the Swabian Alb, near Reutlingen — where the German leg of David's own line came to rest after 1947.
body: Anton Rudolf Defranceski appears on the Pfullingen list of foreigners in 1947 and was certified by that town's mayor in 1950. Pfullingen, Reutlingen, Neuhausen an der Erms, Metzingen and Bad Urach are one small district, and the family's German years happen inside it.
This is the leg of the journey that a walking itinerary is still owed for.

name: Postira
lead: On the north shore of Brač, with three reconstructed households of the name.
body: Postira sits with Omiš and Split in the Dalmatian group. Three households here were reconstructed from indexed records; none has been read register-page by register-page.

name: Santa Maria di Sala
lead: In the Veneto between Padua and Venice — a mainland Venetian parish carrying the name.
body: Six people, from the tree rather than from a register read here. Relevant because the Venetian line of this archive — the printers, the Grand Chancellor, the Omiš and Zadar families — is a Venetian-state story, and mainland parishes of the Republic are where its ordinary people would be.

name: Šterna
lead: Three generations in a hill parish behind Buje — and the answer took one test after the throttle lifted.
body: Šterna had sixteen indexed records on this archive's parish table, 1786–1832, and no book to read them in. It is not one of the parishes walked through the filmed collection, and the note written earlier on 13 September 2026 left it needing «a different route entirely».

The route was one film number and one test. **Film 005497888** carries the records; its catalogue names two parishes on the reel, **Šterna** and **Šumber**. Matched image by image against each parish's own books: **Šterna eleven, Šumber none.**

And it is a household, three generations deep. **Gio Batta De Franceschi and Zanetta Gravisi** — the index writes her surname *Gravisi* once and *Granisi* once — stand behind two entries in the marriage book of 1723–1820 as the parents of the groom. Their son **Bortolo De Franceschi** and his wife, written *Zannetta*, *Zanetta*, *Giovana* and *Giovanna* by four hands, baptise **Felice Anto on 27 September 1778**, **Mariana in February 1786**, **Federico on 14 March 1794** and **Catarina on 11 August 1797**; a Francesco «of Bortolo» is buried on 20 December 1787. Then a second **Gio Batta De Franceschi and Maria** baptise **Federico Felice Antonio on 20 December 1807** and **Cattarina on 7 September 1809**, and bury a **Bartolo** in July 1819.

The grandfather's name coming back round — Gio Batta, Bortolo, Gio Batta, Bartolo — is what this family does everywhere it can be watched, and it is the reason the four of them cannot be told apart by name alone. The register's own books run **1723–1836** and have never been read here.

**Zanetta Gravisi is worth a page of her own if the marriage entry bears her out.** Gravisi is the name of a Capodistrian marquisal house with holdings in this part of Istria. The index gives it twice in two spellings and no date; only the page will say.

name: Vrsar
lead: One household, five entries, sixteen years: a christening, a widowing and a death, and then the name stops.
body: **Francesco De Franceschi and Giacoma** baptise a son, **Luca, on 11 August 1670**. **Giacoma is buried in 1683.** A **Marga «of Francesco»** is buried on 19 August 1686. **Francesco himself is buried on 26 November 1686.**

That is the whole of the name at Vrsar — five entries, three of them burials, inside sixteen years. The parish has four volumes from 1613 and nothing of the family before 1670 or after 1686. A household arrived, was recorded, and ended or moved on.
Orsera is on the coast between Poreč and Rovinj, twelve kilometres from Svetvinčenat, where a De Franceschi household is documented from 1628.

name: Plomin
lead: Above its bay on the eastern Istrian coast, at the Kvarner end of the county of Pazin.
body: Three people of the name. Plomin sits on the road between the Pazin county villages and the Kvarner shore — the same route the Carnia line is inferred to have taken to Fiume.

name: Paluzza
lead: In the Val But of Carnia, on the road to the Plöcken pass — one of the valleys the 1679 headmen's list covers.
body: Paluzza belongs with Mione, Ovaro, Muina and Givigliana in the Carnian group. The documented link to Istria is the 1679 list on which a Zuane De Franceschi of Mione is recorded working in the County of Pazin with his son; Paluzza is on the map because the walking itinerary crosses it, not because a person of the name is yet documented here.

name: Sovinjak
lead: Two burials, twenty-four years apart, and both of them a son of a Gio Battista.
body: The register holds exactly two entries for this parish and they are the whole of what is known. **Zuane Franceschi, buried at Sovignacco in 1759, son of Gio Batta Franceschi.** **Sebastiano De Franceschi, born and buried on 6 August 1783, son of Gio Battista De Franceschi** — an infant, dead in the same year he was born.

One small hill parish above Buzet; two sons of a man of that name a quarter of a century apart. It is either a father who buried a child in middle age and another in old age, or it is two generations putting the grandfather's name back into use — which is what this family does in every place where it can be watched long enough to see.

Neither reading can be tested yet. **Sovinjak is not one of the forty-three Istrian parishes in the filmed collection this archive has walked**, and no register of it has been found on any film reachable from here. The town sits on the Buzet upland with Roč, Hum, Draguč and Šterna — four more parishes carrying the name and three of them equally unfilmed. Until one of those books opens, the household stays a pair of burials and a shared Christian name.

The place was reached not by searching for it but by asking a duller question: which towns in this archive's own register have no entry in this archive's own atlas? Twenty-one did. Sovinjak was one of only five whose rows turned out to carry the family's name at all.

name: Tar
lead: A man of sixty-seven buried here in 1895, and the four-year-old son he had buried twenty-five years before.
body: **Angelus Defranceschi, born 1828, died 23 April 1895 and buried at Tar the following day.** His wife is written only as **Julie**. In the same book, twenty-five years earlier: **Julius, born 1866, dead on 8 March 1870 and buried on the 9th**, son of *Angeli Defranceschi* and *Luciæ Rodella*.

So the wife the burial entry calls Julie is named in the child's entry as **Lucia Rodella**, and the boy was given his mother's name in its masculine form. That is the whole household: one couple, one child who did not live, and a man who outlived the boy by a quarter of a century.

Tar is four volumes in the filmed collection, opening in 1815 — so this household *can* be read, and has not been. It sits in the country behind Poreč with Kaštelir, Vižinada, Šterna and Draguč, the block this archive calls the Poreč hinterland: about sixty entries between them, no lane running through any of them, and not one page read by eye.

name: Pomer
lead: Lucia Defranceschi and Matthaeus Lazar, six children, and a daughter's wedding that closed the circle.
body: Pomer sits on the bay south-east of Pula. It was one of twenty-one towns found on 13 September 2026 to be in this archive's register but not in its atlas — on the strength of three rows, all spelt **Defrančichi**, none of them ours. It has a De Franceschi family in it after all.

**Lucia Defranceschi × Matthaeus Lazar** — the name written *Lazaro*, *Lazar* and *Lazar* by three hands. **Antonius Matheus 1870 · Matheus 1873 · Jacobus 1875 · Zorica «or Albina» 1880 · Josephus 1882 · Catharina 1884.**

And the entry that found her: the wedding of her daughter **Catharina Lazar to Joannes Zuccon**, which had to name the bride's mother and so named Lucia. That is the exact mechanism this archive's «lost daughters» queue was built on — a woman of the name recoverable only because somebody else's marriage needed her in it.
She was one of three different women the index files under «Lucia Defranceschi». The other two are at Vodnjan and Ližnjan.

name: Krbune
lead: One volume, 124 images, and a De Franceschi daughter's whole family inside it.
body: Krbune is a hamlet in the County of Pazin, four kilometres from Gologorica — the same small country this archive's own line lives in. FamilySearch has **one book** of it, 124 images.

That book holds **Mariana De Franceschi and Vincentius Marziol**: **Maria**, **Rosaria** 1833, **Franciscus** 21 November 1836, **Anna** 16 November 1839, **Antonia** 17 March 1843 — and four further entries where the couple stand godparent to other families' children.

She looked like several women because the index spells her husband four ways — *Marziol*, *Marizo*, *Marjas*, *Marjiol* — and her own name *Mariana*, *Marianna*, and in the Croatian orthography of the 1830s **«Marianna Defrančeški»**. One woman, one village, eleven entries.
She is **not** the Mariana De Franceschi born at Šterna in February 1786; that one would have been fifty-seven at the last of these births.

name: Dubrovnik
lead: Fifty-six records with no town written on them, and a family of the name in the old Republic.
body: Dubrovnik is the largest thing in this archive's index that has never had a page. Resolved through the films their images sit on, **fifty-six records** of the name belong to the city parish and to **Pile** outside the western gate — against the twenty-two and sixteen the parish table has carried. Not one of them says «Dubrovnik» in its place field.

The household that can be followed is a **Marietta Defranceschi**, daughter of a **Pietro Defranceschi**, who marries **Matteo Persich** — later written **Peršić** — and whose children are baptised in the city: **Cattarina Teresa Vittoria Maria in 1863** and **Giustino Antonio Alberto Lucciano in 1871**. An Antonio Persich marries a Maria Defranceschi in 1853. The 1829 entry that names Pietro is a marriage, forty-two years before the last of the children, so more than one generation of Persich is in these rows and this page will not pretend to sort them yet.

Nothing joins any of it to the Venetian line at Zadar, Omiš and Imotski, or to Istria. Ragusa was a separate republic with its own patriciate and its own trade, and a Franceschi there needs its own argument, not an inherited one.

name: Labin
lead: The oldest books in the Istrian catalogue — from 1536 — and a family that only shows up three centuries into them.
body: Labin's eleven volumes open in **1536**, the earliest of any Istrian parish FamilySearch has filmed, and they have never been read here.

The archive has carried «Labin 1615 — Aloÿsius Defranceschi» as **the single earliest indexed occurrence of the surname anywhere in Istria**. Read by image against the parish's own books, that entry is not in the pool this archive can see, and the records that *are* run **1826–1866**. The 1615 is not withdrawn — it may sit in a harvest this pass did not reach — but it is not confirmed either, and the honest statement is that Labin's confirmed run begins two centuries later than the page has implied.
Six of the fourteen indexed hits are **Franceschich, Francescich, Francocich** — Slavic formations of the same root, and not this family.

What is here is a married-out daughter and her family: **Dominica Defranceschi × Antonius Zustovich**, with children baptised **1853, 1857, 1861, 1864 and 1866**. Earlier, in 1824 and 1827, a **Maria Defranceschi** stands in two marriage entries as the mother of the parties.

name: Medulin
lead: Four records at the southern tip, and a Maria Defranceschi whose children married Voinich.
body: Medulin is the third of the southern-tip parishes, with Ližnjan and Premantura, and its books open in **1648**.

Four records of the name, and they are marriages rather than baptisms: **Josephus Grahalich in 1828** and **Martinus Rakich in 1831**, both weddings in which a **Maria Defranceschi** and an **Antonius Voinich** stand as the bride's parents; and **Lucas Kivac in 1874**, whose mother is a Maria Defranceschi married to Petrus Kivac.

Which means the De Franceschi presence here is visible **only through daughters** — the surname never appears on a child of the name, only on the mothers of other families' children. It is the clearest small example of what the lost-daughters queue was built to catch.

name: Galižana
lead: One entry, and it carries the surname this archive spent a day chasing at Vodnjan.
body: Galižana holds a single record of the name, a marriage of **1824**, and it is worth a page for what is in it: the groom is **Giacomo Giachin**, and a **Domenica Defranceschi** is named among the parties.

**Giachin** is the surname behind an open question at Vodnjan. A *Michiela De Franceschi fu Giuseppe* is named in the Vodnjan death register of February 1833 as the mother of a **Giacomo Giachin**; and the Vodnjan marriages carry a **Sebastiano Giachin × Domenica De Franceschi**, 1817–1832. Here is a Giacomo Giachin marrying at Gallesano in 1824 with a Domenica Defranceschi in the entry.

The index writes one of the parties as **«Sebastiano Defranceschi»**, which is almost certainly wrong — a Giachin father given the mother's surname by a transcriber, a failure this archive has seen before. **The page will say and the index will not**, and until the page is read this is a coincidence of names in a neighbouring parish and nothing more.
